segments.text: I've talked about how this report on benzene and acne products use really high heat, but
how scared should we be at normal temperatures?
The Valetial Report doesn't specifically tell us the numbers, but if we look at these
graphs we can estimate them from day zero.
Assuming they measured these correctly, it looks like most of them are quite low, but
a few might have about 20 parts per million.
This is 10 times more than a limit the FDA has used before, which isn't great, but
it's less scary than some people are making a sound.
Benzene is actually all around us because it's in fossil fuels.
It's at a thousand parts per million in petrol and it evaporates into the air, it's
also in natural gas and paints and furniture.
Yes, it is a known carcinogen and there's no safe level, but that doesn't mean that
any amount is dangerous.
It means that little bits will add up to increase your risk of cancer.
And even though we all breathe in benzene all the time, the vast majority of us don't
end up with benzene-related cancers.
So let's compare how much benzene we can get from these products to other sources.
Benzene doesn't get through skin easily, so this is how much you would breathe in
if all of the benzene evaporated and then went straight up your nostrils which obviously doesn't
happen. Here's how much is produced when you cook, how much you breathe in when you fill up your
car or just breathing at home. Obviously reducing benzene is a good idea. I'm guessing there might
be some recall soon but there is really no need to freak out. Benzoproxide has been used for acne
for 60 years and there's no recorded increased cancer in people who use it. And compared to
benzene in sunscreen which also wasn't that scary it looks like less benzene. The concentration
was lower in sunscreen, but the amount we use is much higher. And this study didn't find
higher benzene levels in people who use sunscreen.
